Title: First Zone
Description: Living out existence in an abandoned wind turbine high above an endless ocean, ultra tough Fenna (Minis) has become used to surviving alone in the aftermath of a climate catastrophe. But when a violent storm separates her from home, she embarks on an odyssey across the vast wetlands of a post-apocalyptic landscape. Along the way Fenna will encounter other survivors and begin remembering connection, community and a life before the end of the world. Resourcefully and beautifully shot in real Holland locations, debut director Thom Lunshof’s film is thoughtful and unsettling. A unique, compelling and urgent film for our times. – Paul Ridd

Title: Hope
Description:
A rural Korean village is under attack from a mysterious creature laying waste to buildings, vehicles and anyone unfortunate to cross its path. Now it is down to a band of hunters, hapless police and terrified locals to identify the beast and bring it down. 



Making its UK Premiere, this ferociously exciting and entirely unpredictable new film from cult director Na Hong-jin (The Chaser, The Yellow Sea, The Wailing) screens in blistering IMAX for one screening only. An unmissable big screen, big format format experience and one of the most ambitious and thrilling films of the year.

Title: Bodyhackers
Description: Intent on exposing the cosmetics industry for exploiting insecurities through unrealistic beauty standards, an environmental activist falls in love with a ballerina with her own obsession with unattainable beauty, becoming dangerously drawn into the world of underground plastic surgery. Director Carlos Conceicao’s English language debut is deliciously noir-ish body horror in the David Cronenberg mould; a sensual world of beauty and flesh, put under the microscope and the scalpel. – Sam Elder

Title: NFTS Sean Connery Lab Shorts
Description: EIFF is honoured to partner with NFTS Scotland and The Sean Connery Foundation for a second year to present the World Premiere of six short films created via the NFTS Sean Connery Talent Lab. These enterprising, innovative shorts showcase the work of talented emerging filmmakers in Scotland. – Paul Ridd

Title: Experimental Shorts
Description: From haunted objects to living landscapes, these films trace porous boundaries between bodies, matter, memory and space. Traversing archives, protests, ruins and dreams, they invite us into ways of sensing the unstable world we inhabit. – Massimo Iannetti
Warnings: Blood, Death and dying, Suicide, Use of flashing lights/strobe lighting, Violence, No content warnings required

Title: Coming Home
Description: A US Marine Corps captain’s wife (Jane Fonda) finds herself drawn to a paraplegic war vet (Jon Voight) after her husband (Bruce Dern) leaves to fight in Vietnam. By the time her husband returns from the front, each one of them has changed immeasurably. Conceived and produced by Fonda, Coming Home is one of the earliest films to explore the emotional as well as physical consequences of the Vietnam War. Hal Ashby’s compassionate, insightful indictment of the impacts of the conflict is an authentic, richly observed and deeply moving exploration of disillusionment, guilt and complex trauma, featuring extraordinary performances from its Oscar-winning cast. We are delighted to welcome Bruce Dern to introduce this special screening. – Emma Boa

Title: Sea of Glass
Description: After experiencing immense family turmoil in the wake of her husband’s death, a woman seeks solace in a quiet seaside town. There, she forms an unexpected bond with a young woman struggling with her own fractured relationship with her violent father. Together, they confront their turbulent pasts with volatile consequences. Beautifully shot, superbly acted and with a palpable tension that fills every frame, this is a superb thriller and nuanced exploration of female solidarity. – Laura Hague
Warnings: Ableism, Abuse, Blood, Death and dying, Domestic abuse, Graphic descriptions of injury, Homophobia and heterosexism, Language, Nudity, Sexism and misogyny, Substance abuse, Violence

Title: Competition Shorts
Description: Grief and heartbreak juxtaposed with renewal and new beginnings shape this year”s short film competition. With films from across the world including Lithuania, France, Iran and Scotland, and featuring powerhouse performances from some of Britain’s finest acting talents, the programme is a showcase for the power of storytelling within a limited runtime. Competing for the £15,000 prize to aid future projects, each film offers hope for cinema and the next generation of talent. – Lillian Crawford

Title: These Violent Delights
Description: Scottish Ballet’s intoxicating, beautifully realised retelling of the classic Shakespeare tragedy combines stunning choreography, gorgeous costuming and fluid cinematography and movement to create a ballet film with a difference. -Elena Gaitanarou
Warnings: Blood, Death and dying, Mild threat, Substance abuse, Suicide, Use of flashing lights/strobe lighting

Title: The State of Us
Description: Boisterous tearaway Frankie, struggling to come to terms with the inevitability of losing best friend Taylor, impulsively breaks him out of hospice care for one final night of fun and debauchery. But what promises to be a night of hedonism quickly becomes something more complicated for the pair. Beautifully observed and performed by a talented young cast, this witty and wise debut from co-directors Ollie Gardner and Jake Harvey explores male friendship in extreme circumstances, as well as grief and acceptance in a uniquely fresh and humane film full of vigour, life and optimism despite its heartbreaking and moving premise. – Paul Ridd
Warnings: Ableism, Death and dying, Homophobia and heterosexism, Language, Mental illness, Mild threat, Self-harm, Sexism and misogyny, Sexual references, Substance abuse, Suicide, Violence

Title: I Want Your Sex
Description: Stuck in a relationship going nowhere with his girlfriend Minerva (Charli xcx) and confused about his sexuality, frustrated and neurotic twentysomething Elliott (Hoffman) finds himself suddenly at the sexual beck and call of his boss, domineering and ultra-confident art gallery boss Erika (Wilde). Exploring generational differences, sexual politics and queerness with his customary visual panache, fearlessness and affection, iconic director Araki makes a welcome return to feature filmmaking with this hilarious and weirdly moving battle of the sexes. – Paul Ridd

Venue Accessibility



Physical Access to Picturehouse



Access to Picturehouse is step free, with a long shallow ramp from the south to north door. 



The main entrance and Box Office are located on the ground floor, accessible via a ramped, electronically assisted entrance door from Lothian Road. 



Physical Access in Picturehouse



There is step free access to wheelchair spaces and companion seats in Screens 1, 2, 3 and 4.



All seats have armrests, 580mm between armrests, and are joined together.



If you intend to transfer from a wheelchair into a cinema seat, please let the Access Booking Service know when booking so that we can find a seat that best matches your requirements.



Screen 1



Located on the First Floor which can be accessed via a passenger lift. 



Two dedicated wheelchair spaces. There are two aisles and access is level from the passenger lift at the front of the screen.



Screens 2, 3 and 4 are half a level down from the Ground Floor, accessible via a platform lift which is located on the ground floor. 



Screen 2 



Has been upgraded to level access and no longer requires a second platform lift to access.



One dedicated wheelchair space. There is one aisle and access is level from the rear right of the screen. 



Screen 3



One dedicated wheelchair space. There is one aisle and access is slightly sloped from the rear left of the screen. 



Audio



Hearing Induction and Visual Impairment systems are available in all screens using either a neck loop or two-channel infrared stethoset. 



Screen 1 also has a single channel Hearing Induction room loop which does not require infra-red sets. You can connect by switching to the ‘T-coil’ on any row.  



Toilets



There are two accessible toilets, suitable for use with wheelchairs and for changing. 



The first is located next to the Box Office on the Ground Floor with level access between the main entrance doors and the passenger lift. 



The second is located in the corridor leading to Screens 2 and 3, accessible via the stairs or a platform lift. No keys are required to use these toilets. 



The closest changing places toilet is located at Johnnie Walker, a 6 minute walk away on Princes Street.



Assistance Dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome in this venue. 



The Meadows is a ten-minute walk away for the exercise of assistance dogs.

Title: Queen at Sea
Description: When Amanda (Binoche) walks in on her elderly parents in the throes of what appears to be a consensual sexual encounter her instinct is to call the police, believing her mother Leslie (Calder-Marshall) who is suffering from dementia, is incapable of giving consent to husband Martin (Courtenay). As this complex, emotionally devastating and utterly gripping scenario plays out we are asked to question our preconceptions, our ideas and our treatment of the elderly in this devastating and superbly acted film, winner of a Silver Bear at the Berlinale. This is a moral maze filmmaking at its most nuanced and sophisticated. -Paul Ridd

Title: The Last Resort
Description: A sun-drenched Gran Canaria resort becomes the unlikely setting for an urgent moral reckoning. When an unexpected incident leaves a family bound to a refugee in desperate need, nothing that follows is straightforward or comfortable. With lead performances that are raw and utterly compelling, Sødahl directs with precision and humanity, crafting a film as tense as it is timely. One of the most urgent and necessary films of the year. – Sara Cowdell
Warnings: Death and dying, Islamophobia, Racism/colourism/racial slurs, Violence

Title: Body Parts
Description: An older woman, her two daughters and the eldest's on-and-off partner orbit around love, loss, faith, Catholicism and self-worth. 'A sense of groundbreaking experimentation' (Epigram). Body Parts weaves naturalism, surrealism, an engulfing original soundscape and facial mapping projection (by Alensi Studios) to create a bold, character-led production that dissolves boundaries between theatrical narrative and live performance art. Its cutting-edge use of technology serves story and emotion. Intimate, inventive and fundamentally human, Body Parts is a taste of the future of contemporary theatre. Fresh from a sold-out preview in Bristol, it comes to Fringe for one week only.
Warnings: Contains distressing or potentially triggering themes, Scenes of a sexual nature, Strong language/swearing

Title: Ian Patterson & Cathy Rentzenbrink: Reading Remedies
Teaser: We suspect that telling you about the radical importance of reading is a bit preach-to-the-choir. Humour us though, as poet and translator Ian Patterson (Books - A Manifesto) encourages reading past your comfort zone – adding avant-garde poems or a bonkbuster to your shelves, perhaps. He’s joined by journalist and bestseller Cathy Rentzenbrink who, in The Agatha Cure, looks through Christie’s canon, asking: who are books for, why do we read, and why do we sometimes stop? Meanwhile, bestselling author Juno Dawson knows firsthand what it’s like to be the target of censorship; her 2014 YA title, This Book is Gay, is listed as one of the most frequently banned books in the USA. Today, the pair discuss the ‘morality’ of art, and why what we choose to condemn reveals so much about us. Chaired by Sarah Manavis.

Title: Seeksaw
Description: Transforming the stage to a 'meta-lab' of uncertainty, 'who' and 'not sure who' navigate the intersection of spiritual desire and tech-worship. Inspired by the phenomenon of China's youth using AI chatbots as fortune tellers, Seeksaw explores our desperate craving for omniscience and the wanting of control. This funny, existential, original devised performance – part philosophical inquiry into fate, part mutual consulting for dog-shit level anxieties – captures a snapshot of our contemporary era: in a time of no questions or no answers, what is next?

Title: Zakia Sewell & Rebecca Tamás: The Rituals We Share
Teaser: Ancient traditions and folk culture can offer up unique ways to craft our own forms of meaning and connection. Writer and NTS Radio host Zakia Sewell’s Finding Albion questions whether today's new folk revival could unite our increasingly divided country, while Rebecca Tamás’ The Book of Mysteries interrogates how traditional practices can transform our relationship to nature and time. In this enlightening conversation, both authors explore their meditations on the nation’s folklore. Chaired by Jean Menzies.

Title: Borges and Me
Description: In the early 1970s writer and student Jay Parini (Whitehead) finds himself committed to driving blind poet Jorge Luis Borges (Gnecco) across the Scottish countryside. Over the course of an eventful journey the pair form a complex and rich bond, one imbued with poetry, music and melancholy. Beautifully adapted from Parini’s memoir, this gorgeously shot and superbly acted film from director Marc Turtletaub evokes memory, time and place with a remarkably vivid and clear-eyed candour. Title: First Zone
Description: Living out existence in an abandoned wind turbine high above an endless ocean, ultra tough Fenna (Minis) has become used to surviving alone in the aftermath of a climate catastrophe. But when a violent storm separates her from home, she embarks on an odyssey across the vast wetlands of a post-apocalyptic landscape. Along the way Fenna will encounter other survivors and begin remembering connection, community and a life before the end of the world. Resourcefully and beautifully shot in real Holland locations, debut director Thom Lunshof’s film is thoughtful and unsettling. A unique, compelling and urgent film for our times. – Paul Ridd

Title: Out There
Description: Still grieving the disappearance of her scientist father, amateur teenaged astronomer Maz (Stocks) is convinced she has spotted something suspicious hovering above her sleepy Welsh hometown. Recruiting the support of her best mate Little Elis (Moya), UFO-obsessed conspiracy theorist Bryn (Barnard) and local psychic Shifty Gruff (Sheen), Maz and her gang of misfits set out to uncover the truth, one that is far more complex than they might have expected. Breathlessly paced, wittily evoking its 1999 setting via superb music choices, costumes and production design, this charming Welsh debut from director Simon Ryninks is poignant, funny and entirely unpredictable. -Paul Ridd

Title: Snapshot
Description: Newly unearthed footage from late 19th century London reveals the complex fate of an all-ladies ghost-hunting society in this transfixing horror feature debut from director Joseph Archer. Exploring a dangerous city of contradictions with a new technology potentially capable of capturing malevolent supernatural forces, the film throws us into a world of cruelty, violence and press sensationalism, threat always hovering just around the next corner and at the peripheries of the pinhole camera lens. An inventive reimagining of the found footage genre this uniquely strange, scary and distinctive film is guaranteed to provoke, disturb and thrill in equal measure. -Paul Ridd

Description:
How do we tell the stories of our prisoners? Across essay film, fiction, and documentary, this programme explores storytelling as a form of resistance against the silencing and isolation imposed by incarceration. Drawing from Walid Daqqa’s notion of parallel time—the suspended temporality imposed by colonial imprisonment, where prisoners are severed from the linear time of the outside world—the films reveal prison not only as a site of confinement, but as a space where culture, thought, and connection continue to exist. In the context of ongoing struggles around political imprisonment, including the Filton 25 case here in the UK, the programme also asks how narratives of prisoners are constructed, challenged, and reclaimed.

Screened as part of Falastin Film Festival (27—30 August).

About the films

Samira Makki: When Solid Turns To Dust, Or A Note On Liquidity From Palestine

This video essay explores liquidity, and its intermittent leaks, as a poetic and political proposition informing anti-colonial struggles. The essay takes its cue from a letter that political prisoner and martyr Walid Daqqa wrote in 2005 where he theorized Parallel Time under Zionist captivity at a high-security facility known as the Gilboa prison. More than a decade later, the same prison became a marker of the historical escape orchestrated by six Palestinian prisoners. Importantly, the escape became an attestation of the possibility of transgression: the Zionist project, in its high-security doctrine and carceral apparatus, are but an illusion made up of dust, as Mahmoud Al-Arda reiterated. The escape triggered the anxiety of the settler-colony not only as it denoted a leak from the ostensibly impenetrable Parallel Time. Rather, the leak expresses an outright commitment to futurity where there is seemingly none. 

Rakan Mayasi: Bonboné

It is thought that wars and conflicts conquer the essence of body and soul, like the heaving of waves on a rough sea. An imprisoned Palestinian from the resistance forces is serving his time in an Israeli jail. Yearning to see his offspring, he contrives a plot with the help of his spouse. Will his attempt pan out as planned?

Al Jazeera: Walid Daqqa: A Parallel Life

This is the story of Walid Daqqa, one of the longest-serving Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails, told by his immediate family and in voice recordings he made behind bars. From a sharp-minded boy in 1948 Palestine to a clandestine PFLP organiser sentenced to life imprisonment, Daqqa turns his cell into a classroom, a think tank and, eventually, a wedding venue when he marries Sanaa Salama inside Ashkelon prison.

Through intimate testimonies from family, former prisoners and his lawyer, the film explores Walid’s idea of “parallel time” – living both under “tonnes of concrete” and beyond the walls. It recounts the smuggling of his sperm, the birth of his daughter, Milad, and his powerful message to her: hate oppression, not people. As cancer consumes him and Israel refuses his release, Milad’s final chant, “Freedom for our prisoners. For my father”, echoes a struggle that outlives Walid Daqqa’s life.

Following the screening will be a Q+A with Diala Ayesh. Diala Ayesh is a Palestinian lawyer and human rights defender dedicated to advocating for the rights of prisoners and detainees. Her work focuses on providing legal representation to political detainees, visiting prisoners held in Israeli prisons, and documenting violations against them. She has continued this work during the period of intensified restrictions and near-total isolation imposed on Palestinian prisoners following the outbreak of the war on Gaza.

Because of her human rights work, Diala has faced harassment and arrest by both the Palestinian Authority and Israeli authorities. On January 17, 2024, she was arrested by Israeli forces and placed under administrative detention without charge or trial. During her nearly year-long detention, she endured mistreatment and prolonged isolation before being released on January 14, 2025. In recognition of her commitment to defending freedom of expression and human rights, Diala received the 2024 Freedom of Expression Award from Index on Censorship.

Description:
Caught Hold of Nothing offers a glimpse into a performance work in progress by Scottish artist, performer and director Magnus Westwell. Performing with Océane Robin, Westwell plays live violin to exhaustion, building layered environments in which the body moves through emotional states toward catharsis.

Inspired by John Glenday’s poem Vitruvian Man, the work explores absence through cycles of repetition and decay. Music and movement break down and rebuild in tandem, leading to a vulnerable, cathartic, and deeply embodied experience that invites audiences into the liminal space of experimental interdisciplinary performance.

The performance will begin the festival’s opening night and launch party. It leads on to a bold late-night celebration in collaboration with Cardion Arts, headlined by rapper and poet Mykki Blanco. Over the past decade, Blanco has evolved from a video-art persona into a pioneering voice in music, blending noise, club, and trap while challenging the boundaries of hip-hop and its dominant narratives. Entering a new chapter, their work continues to push sound and identity into unexpected territory. 

Taking over the Biscuit Factory late into the night, the opening party will also see DJ sets from 3MR, a Syrian-Scottish multidisciplinary artist and curator of POC-focused events in Scotland, and Sweet Philly, a Dublin-born, Edinburgh-based producer and DJ, and self-styled ‘Queer Club Demon’. An immersive start to the festival, the opening night brings together performance, club culture, and collective experience, setting the tone for a programme defined by bold ideas and boundary-breaking creativity.

Title: Gaza: What Still Grows
Teaser: Set against the backdrop of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, these three films are united by an insistence on creating life under conditions designed to destroy it. Whether tending the land, building new technologies of care, or performing for children, they present creation not as an escape from genocide, but as a refusal to let […]
Description:
Set against the backdrop of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, these three films are united by an insistence on creating life under conditions designed to destroy it. Whether tending the land, building new technologies of care, or performing for children, they present creation not as an escape from genocide, but as a refusal to let it define the limits of Palestinian life.

Screened as part of Falastin Film Festival (27—30 August).

About the films

Woroud Alqassas: Seeds & Roots

Here, where gunpowder is mixed with soil, Seba kneels to cleanse the soil from the ashes of war, watering it with her small cup trying to revive memories buried in the seeds. Besides her stands her grandfather, Abu Diaa, his voice is rough as the land, rooted like an old olive tree. He knows the land and the land knows him. He teaches her that planting is a promise of life despite all forms of death. Together, they help their land to breathe again, each green leaf they grow together becomes a new birth certificate.



Maria Marone: Rendered In Light

When Mosab, a skilled software engineer, is separated from his wife and children as they evacuate Gaza for emergency medical care, he’s left behind with only uncertainty and a laptop. Alone in a city under siege, he begins building something extraordinary: a virtual reality program designed to help survivors of genocide cope with mental trauma. As genocide rages around him, Mosab immerses himself in creating digital worlds of calm and reflection. The film follows his journey as he balances the emotional weight of his own loneliness with a relentless drive to serve others. Through acts of kindness and innovation, he finds a way to preserve his own mental health, turning grief into action, and despair into purpose.

Mai Saad + Ahmed Al Danaf: One More Show

Amidst the devastation of the genocide carried by Israel in Gaza, a group of circus performers refuse to let despair take center stage. One More Show follows The Free Gaza troupe; Youssef, Batout, Ismail, Mohamed and Just, after being displaced from northern to southern Gaza , as they turn their craft into an act of defiance, resilience, and hope. As death hovers in the background, the troupe performs for children in shelters and on the streets, offering moments of joy in the darkest of times.

Title: Gaza: Against The Perfect Victim
Teaser: Inspired by Mohammed El-Kurd’s critique of the “perfect victim,” this programme brings together two films that refuse the narrow roles so often assigned to Palestinian men. Across life before and during Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, they offer intimate portraits of men in all their contradictions – playful, vulnerable, stubborn, imperfect, and deeply ordinary – […]
Description:
Inspired by Mohammed El-Kurd’s critique of the “perfect victim,” this programme brings together two films that refuse the narrow roles so often assigned to Palestinian men. Across life before and during Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, they offer intimate portraits of men in all their contradictions – playful, vulnerable, stubborn, imperfect, and deeply ordinary – insisting on the right to be seen as fully human rather than as symbols to be judged.

Screened as part of Falastin Film Festival (27—30 August).

About the films

Bisan Owda: Free Fish

Free Fish is an intimate short documentary filmed entirely in Gaza during one of the deadliest years in recent history. The film follows two brothers, Mohammad and Ahmad Kaloob, separated by siege and displacement, yet bound by the sea. Mohammad, displaced in Khan Younis with his two young daughters, fishes from the South and tries to find alternatives for the boat and net he lost in the bombing of Gaza Seaport. Ahmad, still in the North under total blockade, risks his life each morning near the Al-Shate’e refugee camp, what was once a livelihood is now a daily act of survival, the coastline is militarized, boats are shot at and hunger is used as a weapon of war.

And yet, the brothers return to the sea. They cast their nets and their memories, into waters that no longer offer freedom, but still carry meaning. Fishing becomes a fragile ritual of resistance, of connection, of presence. The film also follows Rami, Mohammad’s teenage nephew, who lost his twin brother during the genocide and now fishes alone. Through him, Free Fish becomes not just a story of survival, but of grief, inheritance, and the quiet defiance of those who refuse to disappear.

Mahmoud Nabil Ahmed: Gazan Tales

In the heart of the beloved Gaza Strip, four men navigate through divergent paths in pursuit of their own definitions of existence, intertwining their fates amidst the complexities of life, love, and survival. As the film unfolds, viewers are immersed in the daily lives of these men, observing how they navigate their routines alongside their families in their beloved city.

Description:
When return is interrupted, memory finds other routes. Bringing together three experimental films, this programme traces how voices, maps, and imagined conversations become ways of navigating inaccessible homelands, preserving collective memory, and sustaining relationships to places that can no longer be reached, but are never left behind. 

Screened as part of Falastin Film Festival (27—30 August).

About the films

Jayce Salloum: untitled part 3b: (as if) beauty never ends..

A more ambient work of many things, including orchids blooming, and flowers growing, superimposed over raw footage from post massacre filmings of the 1982 slaughter at Sabra and Shatila refugee camp in Lebanon. Cloud footage, Hubbell space imagery, the visible body crosscuts, and abstract shots of slow motion water, add to this reflection of the past, its present context and foreshadowing trajectory. With the voice over of Abdel Majid Fadl Ali Hassan (a 1948 refugee living in Bourg El Barajneh camp) recounting a story told by the rubble of his home in Palestine, and the collection of audio accompanying the clips, the tape permeates into an intense essay on dystopia in contemporary times. Working directly, viscerally, and metaphorically the videotape provides an elegiac response to the ongoing Palestinian dispossession & genocide.

Hajar Ibrahim: Memory Is a Stranger (Flowers of Sudden Return)

Memory is a Stranger (Flowers of a Sudden Return) is a short archival-experimental documentary assembled from family footage filmed by the filmmaker’s late grandfather in Gaza’s Nuseirat Refugee Camp, alongside an auditory landscape gathered over several years and made up entirely from her own recordings archiving the families oral testimonies and gatherings, protests, family folkloric songs, and field recordings. Unable to return herself, the filmmaker turns to Google Earth as part of an earlier Palestinian practice of digital return, echoing Darby’s 2006 “Nakba Layer,” which used satellite imagery to help refugees ‘visit’ destroyed and existing Palestinian villages. The film follows her two grandmothers oral testimonies of defiantly enacting a return home to Jerusalem and Gaza despite the occupation’s restrictions and siege. The film foregrounds less-recounted histories of return rather than displacement, tracing memory as a layered absence that is continually mediated generationally. Across three generations, return is enacted and remembered differently: by her grandmothers through physical acts of return, by her mother through lived memories of Gaza reawakened by family footage, and by the filmmaker through an inherited memory that becomes the film itself.

Razan AlSalah: A Stone’s Throw

Amine, a Palestinian elder, is exiled twice, from land and labor, from Haifa to Beirut to a Gulf offshore oil platform. A Stone’s Throw trespasses borders to reveal an emotional and material proximity between the extraction of oil and labour in the region and the Zionist colonization of Palestine. The film rehearses a history of the Palestinian resistance when, in 1936, the oil labourers of Haifa blow up a BP pipeline.

Description:
Lebanon, July 2006. War is raging between Hezbollah and Israel. During a 24h ceasefire, Marwan heads out in search of his father who refused to leave his Southern village and leaves his wife Rana preparing alone their immigration to Canada. Marwan finds no traces of his father and the ceasefire is quickly broken, forcing him to take shelter in Najib’s house, his father’s friend. Marwan finds himself trapped under the rain of bombs with Najib and a group of elders, friends of his father. Tension rises inside and outside of the house. Suddenly, a group of Israeli soldiers enter the first floor. The next three days sees the situation spiral out of control.

Screened as part of Falastin Film Festival (27—30 August).

Followed by an online Q&A with the director.

Title: Grace Mulvey: Gigantica
Description: Grace has a massive head. Physically. Not egotistically. Grace dares to tackle a controversial topic – is it an insult to tell a woman she looks like her Dad? From her toddler niece getting a boyfriend before her to embracing millennial women’s religion (going woo woo) to her Dad’s memory slipping and Grace’s big face being the only one he recognises. This warm and laugh-out-loud show is about parents, identity, and finding joy in the things you can’t escape. 'Guaranteed floor-to-ceiling laughs' (BeyondTheJoke.co.uk). Title: Scout Boxall: God's Favourite
Description: Melbourne International Comedy Festival 2025 Most Outstanding Show nominee, Pinder Prize winner. Stranded in regional Victoria without medication for the first time in 12 years, Scout pulls out all the psychological stops to survive the worst night of their life. An exquisite, darkly funny retelling of a harrowing mental marathon through manic withdrawal; Scout imagines life in the Middle Ages, trawls the strange crevices of the internet, makes peace with their own mediocrity and (briefly) surrenders to God. Part storytelling, part stand-up, all raw and unflinchingly real. ***** (Time Out). **** (Chortle.co.uk). **** (List).

Title: The Front List: Special Edition – John Grisham

Chances are you’ll find a copy of The Client, The Rainmaker, or A Time To Kill on your own bookshelf – or you'll have caught one of his blockbuster film adaptations starring Tom Cruise (The Firm) or Julia Roberts (The Pelican Brief). Description:
Join Trans Masc Studies’ Ellis Jackson Kroese for a deep dive into the film archive of Del LaGrace Volcano, screening a selection of works exploring queer identity, BDSM culture, and embodied politics. Bringing together documentary footage, experimental film, and archival material, the screening traces Volcano’s influential role within queer and trans visual culture across several decades.

In this joint screening and in-conversation between the two artists, Jackson Kroese weaves Volcano’s work into their ongoing practice of preserving and activating trans histories, considering the archive as a living site of memory, community, and resistance. The event will open space for reflection on how queer and trans lives are documented, shared, and sustained through moving image practices.

Listen to chilling tales of executions, grave robbers and ghostly encounters as you ride through the Old and New Towns. This theatrical tour brings Edinburgh’s gruesome history to life with gallows humour, eerie stories and a touch of the supernatural.

Title: Danger Plan!
Description: Sophia’s family has always had a plan. A way out. A route to survive. She assumed everyone did, until she asked her friends, 'what do you want to do if there’s a catastrophe?' and they stared at her like she had three heads. Her family’s caution came from a real place, and multiple generations were raised with the mantra: 'You have to be ready to run.' Danger Plan! is part solo show and part cabaret, featuring personal stories, original songs, and dark humour exploring generational trauma, anxiety, and the absurdities of living in uncertain times.

Hannah is the co-host and creator of the hit podcast Ghost Huns with over 5 million listens and 1.3 million followers on TikTok. NTA winner. TV also includes The Stand-Up Sketch Show (ITV2) and Celebrity Weakest Link (BBC One). 'Want to howl with laughter? See Hannah. She is a comedy goddess' (Claudia Winkleman).

Screens 1 and 2 are accessible to customers with limited mobility, including wheelchair users. There are four wheelchair spaces in Screen 1 and two in Screen 2.



Dedicated wheelchair spaces are available in the following locations:



Screen 1: Row M, Seats 1-2 & 20-21



Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11



Aisles in our screens are located on each side of every row:



Screen 1: aisles are located next to seats A1 – M21 or seats A20, C20, E20, G20, J20, L20.



Screen 2: aisles are located next to seats A1-C1, A15, B16, and C18.



Sofa seats are double seats with no armrest in between. These are sold as two seats and are located:



Screen 1: No sofa seats



Screen 2: B1+2, B3+4, B13+14, B15+16, C1+2, C3+4, C15+16, C17+18



All seats have immovable armrests, and chairs are fixed together.



The distance of the aisles between seats – from the front of one row of seats to the back of another – is approximately 50cm. The seat base and back are approx 48cm wide; 69cm wide including armrests.



The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.

Title: Darren McGarvey: Trauma Industrial Complex

Chaired by Ali Millar.

Title: The Understudy
Description: Exploring the anxiety-fuelled existence of an Australian swing, this one-woman catastrophe follows an understudy who's put everything on hold for her moment in the spotlight. She'll do anything for the stage... no matter the cost. Subversive, silly and unflinchingly honest, The Understudy traverses jealousy, self-righteousness and the price of ambition in a hauntingly dark comedy that turns on a dime. It's 'surreal and hilarious' **** (List) and 'unexpectedly moving, and sharply observed' ****½ (FIFTY+SA). Winner: Weekly Award for Best Theatre (Adelaide Fringe 2026). Written and performed by Eva Seymour. Directed by Olivia Charalambous.

Venue Accessibility



Physical Access to the Cameo



Both the bar and main entrance are wheelchair accessible. However, level access to the bar is only available from the street through the Lochrin Place entrance – moving between the two areas requires a wheelchair user to enter via the street.



Physical Access in the Screening Rooms



Screens 1 and 2 are accessible to customers with limited mobility, including wheelchair users. There are four wheelchair spaces in Screen 1 and two in Screen 2.



Dedicated wheelchair spaces are available in the following locations:



Screen 1: Row M, Seats 1-2 & 20-21



Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11



Aisles in our screens are located on each side of every row:



Screen 1: aisles are located next to seats A1 – M21 or seats A20, C20, E20, G20, J20, L20.



Screen 2: aisles are located next to seats A1-C1, A15, B16, and C18.



Sofa seats are double seats with no armrest in between. These are sold as two seats and are located:



Screen 1: No sofa seats



Screen 2: B1+2, B3+4, B13+14, B15+16, C1+2, C3+4, C15+16, C17+18



All seats have immovable armrests, and chairs are fixed together.



The distance of the aisles between seats – from the front of one row of seats to the back of another – is approximately 50cm. The seat base and back are approx 48cm wide; 69cm wide including armrests.



The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.

Title: What's Happening Now?
Description: The panel show bringing comics, journalists, wise women and clueless men together to figure out: What's Happening Now? A comedy compilation for people who want to care about the world, but are exhausted by it. Based on the podcast of the same name, WHN has been called QI meets Have I Got News For You and now, for the first time, a live audience helps tackle the biggest questions, curiosities and stories befuddling the world. Previous guests include Rosie Holt, Stuart Goldsmith, the former director of BBC News and a Tory activist who campaigns by downing pints.

Title: Uncorked
Description: Best friends since primary school, Kate and Nadia hold tightly to their sacred monthly ritual of cheap wine and bad TV – a tradition born in their teens and clung to ever since. But as their mid-twenties loom, the cracks in both their lives and the tradition begin to spill open. Kate is afraid of moving forward. Nadia is afraid of falling behind. With three potential fathers and the clock ticking, this Friday is a little different from usual. Uncorked explores fertility, friendship and falling out of sync with your own life.
Warnings: Contains distressing or potentially triggering themes, Strong language/swearing

The audience chooses a new setting for the story, curveballs in scenes, and some members will get the responsibility of triggering songs, challenges and more! Chaos will ensue as the story you know and love is affectionately twisted in a way not even the performers will see coming.

Physical Access to Picturehouse



Access to Picturehouse is step free, with a long shallow ramp from the south to north door. 



The main entrance and Box Office are located on the ground floor, accessible via a ramped, electronically assisted entrance door from Lothian Road. 



Physical Access in Picturehouse



There is step free access to wheelchair spaces and companion seats in Screens 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Screens 2, 3 and 4 are half a level down from the Ground Floor, accessible via a platform lift which is located on the ground floor. 



Screen 2

Screen 3

Title: Northbound
Description: Frustrated with living out his final days in a nursing home, elderly rogue Arthur (Dern) recruits his uptight grandson Kevin (Parrish) to break him out. Together the pair head north to Canada, picking up an enigmatic stranger (Fox) along the way. Acidly funny, unpredictable and ultimately very moving, this sharply directed and superbly acted film from director William Scoular is a showcase for Bruce Dern’s magnetic screen presence and feeling for a character who positively bursts off the screen. Featuring a final performance from legendary actor Graham Greene as well as superb supporting turns from Joanna Cassidy and Dylan Baker. -Paul Ridd

Physical Access to Picturehouse

There is step free access to wheelchair spaces and companion seats in Screens 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Screen 1



Located on the First Floor which can be accessed via a passenger lift.

Has been upgraded to level access and no longer requires a second platform lift to access.

Screen 3

Audio



Hearing Induction and Visual Impairment systems are available in all screens using either a neck loop or two-channel infrared stethoset. 



Screen 1 also has a single channel Hearing Induction room loop which does not require infra-red sets. You can connect by switching to the ‘T-coil’ on any row.  



Toilets



There are two accessible toilets, suitable for use with wheelchairs and for changing. 



The first is located next to the Box Office on the Ground Floor with level access between the main entrance doors and the passenger lift. 



The second is located in the corridor leading to Screens 2 and 3, accessible via the stairs or a platform lift. No keys are required to use these toilets. 



The closest changing places toilet is located at Johnnie Walker, a 6 minute walk away on Princes Street.



Assistance Dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome in this venue. 



The Meadows is a ten-minute walk away for the exercise of assistance dogs.

Title: The Mad World of Harvey Kurtzman
Description: A vivid, immersive and visually striking portrait of the founder of the satirical publication Mad magazine and its far-reaching influence on some of the most prominent artists of our time. Kurtzman’s commitment to integrity and challenging the status quo with humour, edge and resilience is a hymn for our times. Rich in historical context, artistic expression, contemporary politics and artfully weaving thoughtful reflections from contributors including Terry Gilliam, the late Stan Lee and Robert Crumb, this is a compelling, insightful exploration of counterculture, commerce and creative compromise and the power of conviction in raw truth and honesty. – Emma Boa

Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11

The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.

Description: Three estranged siblings reunite in rural Italy after the middle sister has been released from psychiatric treatment following a breakdown, one she experienced as a deep spiritual awakening. Title: The Education of Jane Cumming
Description:
In early nineteenth-century Edinburgh, two women run a girls’ boarding school, trying to build an independent life in a world with little room for women outside convention. When a wealthy grandmother enrols her granddaughters, including 15-year-old Jane Cumming, the school’s fragile balance begins to shift. Jane’s isolation, the teachers’ concern and the pressures of respectability soon lead to an accusation that changes all their lives. Based on true events, Sophie Heldman’s beautifully made period drama explores prejudice, reputation and the cost of surviving in a strict and unforgiving society. – Annita Nitsaidou
Presented by Reclaim The Frame
Warnings: Homophobia and heterosexism, Racism/colourism/racial slurs, Sexism and misogyny

Title: The Mad World of Harvey Kurtzman
Description: A vivid, immersive and visually striking portrait of the founder of the satirical publication Mad magazine and its far-reaching influence on some of the most prominent artists of our time. Kurtzman’s commitment to integrity and challenging the status quo with humour, edge and resilience is a hymn for our times. Rich in historical context, artistic expression, contemporary politics and artfully weaving thoughtful reflections from contributors including Terry Gilliam, the late Stan Lee and Robert Crumb, this is a compelling, insightful exploration of counterculture, commerce and creative compromise and the power of conviction in raw truth and honesty. – Emma Boa
Warnings: Death and dying, Sexism and misogyny, Sexual references, Suicide, War

Title: Sacred Creatures
Description: Three estranged siblings reunite in rural Italy after the middle sister has been released from psychiatric treatment following a breakdown, one she experienced as a deep spiritual awakening. As this troubled young woman behaves more erratically and relationships fracture, the local community takes on an unexpected significance as power dynamics shift and change. Frieda Luk’s artfully composed and highly compelling debut feature is a deftly woven, unpredictable and black-humoured thriller of superstition, idolatry and communal faith with a distinctive magical realist edge. – Emma Boa

Title: Northbound
Description: Frustrated with living out his final days in a nursing home, elderly rogue Arthur (Dern) recruits his uptight grandson Kevin (Parrish) to break him out. Together the pair head north to Canada, picking up an enigmatic stranger (Fox) along the way. Acidly funny, unpredictable and ultimately very moving, this sharply directed and superbly acted film from director William Scoular is a showcase for Bruce Dern’s magnetic screen presence and feeling for a character who positively bursts off the screen. Featuring a final performance from legendary actor Graham Greene as well as superb supporting turns from Joanna Cassidy and Dylan Baker. -Paul Ridd

Venue Accessibility



Physical Access to the Cameo



Both the bar and main entrance are wheelchair accessible. However, level access to the bar is only available from the street through the Lochrin Place entrance – moving between the two areas requires a wheelchair user to enter via the street.



Physical Access in the Screening Rooms



Screens 1 and 2 are accessible to customers with limited mobility, including wheelchair users. There are four wheelchair spaces in Screen 1 and two in Screen 2.



Dedicated wheelchair spaces are available in the following locations:



Screen 1: Row M, Seats 1-2 & 20-21



Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11



Aisles in our screens are located on each side of every row:



Screen 1: aisles are located next to seats A1 – M21 or seats A20, C20, E20, G20, J20, L20.



Screen 2: aisles are located next to seats A1-C1, A15, B16, and C18.



Sofa seats are double seats with no armrest in between. These are sold as two seats and are located:



Screen 1: No sofa seats



Screen 2: B1+2, B3+4, B13+14, B15+16, C1+2, C3+4, C15+16, C17+18



All seats have immovable armrests, and chairs are fixed together.



The distance of the aisles between seats – from the front of one row of seats to the back of another – is approximately 50cm. The seat base and back are approx 48cm wide; 69cm wide including armrests.



The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.

Description:
The Community Wellbeing Collective (CWC) hosts a creative gathering to celebrate the work of prolific photographer and community worker Sandra George. George’s photos captured Edinburgh through the 80s and 90s, presenting an intimate portrait of the people she worked with across Wester Hailes and Craigmillar. Her work is held in archive at Craigmillar Now.

Led by Craigmillar Now’s lead archivist and CWC member Anna Mayhew, the event offers a close look at the artist’s local photography, alongside a shared meal featuring cyanotype tablecloths, a photography workshop creating a collective installation, and sharing memories of the communities George documented. This is part of a series of Anchor Events: CWC’s monthly explorations bringing together a diverse community connected to Wester Hailes, with local organisations and artists.

Were these errors accidents, ambition, propaganda or fear of empty space? Along the way, see how trade, empire, faith and imagination bent geography. Through projected maps, story and music, this show reveals how cartographers got it wrong, and what their errors reveal about us.

Teaser: In an age of conflict, conspiracies, and unchecked AI generation, having news sources we can trust has never been more vital. But how does our media maintain balance on such rocky ground? Title: The Inside Scoop on Investigations
Teaser: There is no better definition of good information than diligent, impartial, well-resourced investigative journalism, where rumours are sifted from verified facts which lead to action. Discussing this most specialised of fields are a panel including Guardian journalist Harry Davies, Centre for Investigative Journalism chair Isabel Hilton and Lucia Osborne-Crowley, whose acclaimed book, The Lasting Harm: Witnessing the Trial of Ghislaine Maxwell, draws on firsthand court reporting from one of the most high-profile cases in living memory. Chaired by Peter Godwin.

Title: Polly Barton & Aea Varfis-van Warmelo: Lies, Crushes, and Karaoke
Teaser: Obsession and karaoke. Lies and self-sabotage. In What Am I, A Deer? and Attention-Seeking Behaviour, Polly Barton and Aea Varfis-van Warmelo bring fierce formal invention to two bitingly funny, mercilessly perceptive novels about trying to translate yourself into someone more palatable. Barton, the fearlessly original essayist and translator of Asako Yuzuki's bestselling Butter, joins Varfis-van Warmelo - a sharp, edgy new voice in fiction - to unpick confession, compulsion, authenticity, and whether we can ever truly escape ourselves. Chaired by Irenosen Okojie.

Title: Colin Bramwell & Ryan Van Winkle: Poetry in Practice
Teaser: Two singular voices in Scottish poetry, Colin Bramwell and Ryan Van Winkle, join the Festival to share new work and discuss their practice of bringing poetry to wider audiences, both on and off the page. Both poets play with questions of communication and connection: Bramwell’s Fetch explores the boundaries of Scots and English to question a host of binaries, while Van Winkle’s intimate Get Closer considers how we remember and misremember, shaping memory through experience. Chaired by Ellen Renton.

Title: Jacek Dukaj & Ursula Phillips: Ice
Teaser: In Jacek Dukaj's Ice, the Tunguska asteroid has plunged the world into eternal winter, freezing not just the land but history itself. A Polish mathematician is sent deep into a transformed Siberia - and into one of the most inventive alternate histories ever written. Joining Dukaj is translator Ursula Phillips, whose remarkable English translation navigates the novel’s intricate tensions between Polish, Russian, and a deranged reality. Together they explore the art of carrying audacious imagined worlds across languages. Chaired by Uilleam Blacker.

Title: ERAS
Description: ERAS: no stadium, no backup dancer, no glitter (not much talent either). A woman traces her life through ten Eras. From childhood chaos to a wedding in Edinburgh, this solo show blends storytelling, cultural commentary and dark humour. Just one woman reclaiming her narrative. Set against cultural shifts from 9/11 to #MeToo to COVID and beyond, this solo autobiographical piece explores trauma, generational inheritance, addiction, academia, love and the radical act of choosing yourself. Blending sharp political observation with intimate confession, ERAS examines what we carry, what we inherit and what we refuse to pass on.

In this darkly funny and deeply personal solo show, Tabatha examines the absurd mechanics of survival: how we process trauma, where language breaks down and why humour sometimes becomes the only way through. A bold, intimate story about resilience.

Description:
In this group exhibition, four emerging artists selected for the inaugural Blackie House Graduate Awards respond to a selection of maps, globes and books held in the Blackie House Library and Museum. 

Artists Milly Toplis, Eve Giltinan Allais, Elena Nieva, and Alyth Krzyzanowska will chart Scotland’s land and seascapes: its hills, mountains and valleys, its lochs, rivers and canals, its paths and roads, its windmills and oil rigs, coastline and islands.

In the age of GPS, the new commissions consider what positions creative minds occupy in and around these natural and man-made features, finding their points of orientation across various media. Told individually and collectively, their stories will take shape in the Blackie House’s unique satellite space: a 250-year-old garage.

Here's some funny keyboard songs. Hate funny songs? Weird. Back to the jokes. Previous reviews and accolades: 'Incredibly clever' **** (BroadwayBaby.com). 'Sharp and witty' **** (EdFestMag.com). 'Quick wit, and vibrant energy' **** (BroadwayWorld.com). 'Unique and charmingly chaotic' **** (TheReviewsHub.com). Edinburgh Fringe Comedian of the Year 2025 nominee. Best Jokes of the Fringe: The Times, The Telegraph and The Scotsman. Seen on ITV and BBC iPlayer.
Venue description: Edinburgh’s premier party venue and the central Free Fringe hub. Four rooms of free shows running throughout the day and night, and a buzzing and vibrant courtyard in the centre of the Cowgate. The Three Sisters boasts a wide variety of food and drinks, with plenty of space to relax during the day and party throughout the night! Shows run from 10:00 – 02:00.

Title: Autism Mama
Description: Welcome to the world of a mother to a pubescent teenager – who happens to be autistic. A fascinating and hilarious stand-up show about a single mum guiding her autistic son through the first stages of puberty. Expect visual aids, balloons, and a heart-warming insight into the relationship between a mother and her son. A show not to be missed! 'Unmissable' (Guardian). 'Her timing is perfect' (WhatsOnStage.co.uk).

Title: Sunshine on Leith
Description: Captivate Theatre's five-star, vibrant, energetic, emotional sell-out production is in the Music Hall! By Stephen Greenhorn, the story follows Ally and Davy as they negotiate families, friendships and love in this funny and moving story featuring songs of The Proclaimers. 'Toe-tapping and filled with hometown love, Captivate Theatre's production of Sunshine on Leith... is fun and energetic.' (AllEdinburghTheatre.com). 'The show has found a very appropriate home at the Edinburgh Fringe, offering audiences a chance to see a musical that really reflects the spirit of city life' (KatMasterson.com).

Title: Katie Norris: Mother Succubus
Description: Boys of the manosphere: prepare to be spooked. Women with cats: your leader has returned. Last year's Best Show Edinburgh Comedy Awards nominee is back and ready for a new era. A stand-up, musical comedy show about maturing adorably from the self-appointed Godmother to the Nation. As seen and heard on 8 Out of 10 Cats Does Countdown (Channel 4). Nominee: Edinburgh Comedy Award Best Show 2025. Nominee: Next Big Thing 2025. Winner: Best Show Leicester 2025. Winner: Musical Comedy Awards 2023. 'Oddball songs, surreal asides and a glorious persona' **** (Guardian). **** (Scotsman). **** (Standard).

Title: Julian Clary: Fully Dilated
Description: It's too early for filth, so think cucumber sandwiches and cream teas. No, not cucumbers, in case I accidentally shove one up my jacksie. Old habits die hard. I've decided to open up to the public and reveal all. No more hiding behind a stage persona; I'm going to be myself. The question is will you be able to tell the difference? In this show I'll reveal intimate secrets of my life and share the traumas that have led me to lead the life of a camp comic and renowned homosexual. 'A tsunami of smut' (Guardian).

Title: Afrique En Cirque
Description: A show by Yamoussa Bangoura, inspired by daily life in Guinea. This performance shares the beauty, youth and artistry of African culture. A colourful show beyond its scenery, costumes and staging, that will make any theatre vibrate with energy. It represents strength, agility and life's joys of young Africans. The audience will see our acrobats execute gravity defying moves and human pyramids, all to the contemporary sounds of Afro-Jazz, percussion and Kora. Welcome to the universe of Kalabanté Productions and prepare for an unforgettable journey.

Title: First Zone
Description: Living out existence in an abandoned wind turbine high above an endless ocean, ultra tough Fenna (Minis) has become used to surviving alone in the aftermath of a climate catastrophe. But when a violent storm separates her from home, she embarks on an odyssey across the vast wetlands of a post-apocalyptic landscape. Along the way Fenna will encounter other survivors and begin remembering connection, community and a life before the end of the world. Resourcefully and beautifully shot in real Holland locations, debut director Thom Lunshof’s film is thoughtful and unsettling. A unique, compelling and urgent film for our times. – Paul Ridd

By Bus and Tram

Princes Exchange | EH3 9BL



What 3 Words for car park entrance location: ///skill.fats.things



146 spaces



Due to the city centre location there is very limited on-street parking with time restrictions. 



Refer to Edinburgh City Council’s parking guide for more information and on-street parking locations and accessible parking bays. 







Venue Accessibility



Physical Access to the Cameo



Both the bar and main entrance are wheelchair accessible. However, level access to the bar is only available from the street through the Lochrin Place entrance – moving between the two areas requires a wheelchair user to enter via the street.



Physical Access in the Screening Rooms



Screens 1 and 2 are accessible to customers with limited mobility, including wheelchair users. There are four wheelchair spaces in Screen 1 and two in Screen 2.



Dedicated wheelchair spaces are available in the following locations:



Screen 1: Row M, Seats 1-2 & 20-21



Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11



Aisles in our screens are located on each side of every row:



Screen 1: aisles are located next to seats A1 – M21 or seats A20, C20, E20, G20, J20, L20.



Screen 2: aisles are located next to seats A1-C1, A15, B16, and C18.



Sofa seats are double seats with no armrest in between. These are sold as two seats and are located:



Screen 1: No sofa seats



Screen 2: B1+2, B3+4, B13+14, B15+16, C1+2, C3+4, C15+16, C17+18



All seats have immovable armrests, and chairs are fixed together.



The distance of the aisles between seats – from the front of one row of seats to the back of another – is approximately 50cm. The seat base and back are approx 48cm wide; 69cm wide including armrests.



The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.







Further Information



Cameo Picturehouse contact details



By Phone: Picturehouse’s dedicated accessibility line 02072 947908 (Text Relay call 18001 02072 947908).



By Email: Use the email form on Picturehouse’s website here.

Title: Capsized
Description: An apparently idyllic house boat trip is thrown into disarray when Diane (Rabe) and her children are rocked by revelations of financial strife kept secret by obstinate husband Ray (Ifans). At sea and with a chaotic holiday ahead of them, the family must struggle to keep it together and face an uncertain future, but not before competing in a truly epic fishing competition. With an easygoing charm, affection for its complex characters, and a real sense of place, Lindsey Ryan’s beautifully filmed and hilarious American indie debut tackles a very contemporary story of economic uncertainty with optimism, warmth and humour. – Paul Ridd

Title: Introduction to Graphic Novels: A Workshop with Lizzy Stewart
Teaser: Lizzy Stewart (author-illustrator of the breathtaking, genre-defying books The Wreck, Alison, and Walking Distance) introduces you today to the world of graphic storytelling. During this hand-on session, you’ll look at character, how to find inspiration, and the way that time can bend and stretch within a graphic novel or comic book. All of this will come together in a short-form comic strip which could form the basis of your own future full-length masterpiece.

Title: Lawrence of Arabia and ME
Description: Hollywood needed a cast of thousands, David Lean, and won seven Oscars. Eamonn Gearon had a camel called Osama. This Oxford-trained historian spent decades in the Middle East – living with Bedu, risking his neck and uncovering secrets Britain buried with Lawrence. History and comedy collide; a sharper image emerges. Neither villain nor hero, but something more interesting. What was promised? What was broken? What would Lawrence make of Peter O’Toole’s performance? With the wit of a raconteur and authority of a scholar, Gearon, 'a masterful storyteller' (TheGreatCourses.com) reveals man, myth, movie... plus camels.
Venue description: Another high-calibre venue. Two classy spaces, alternatives to the Fringe norm, boasting the most comfortable seats in town! Wonderfully located in our 11-space hub adjacent to theSpaceTriplex and theSpace @ Surgeons' Hall. A programme of music, a capella, theatre, improv, sketch and comedy and a stylish garden bar in the adjacent square. A must for all well-heeled theatre-goers.

Title: Wally Baram: My Snake's Quinceañera
Description: Star of hit Amazon series Overcompensating, don’t miss Wally Baram’s first ever UK tour dates! Wally was named a Just For Laughs ‘New Face’ of stand-up comedy, made her late-night debut on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, and has written for Apple TV's Shrinking. She earned a 2026 Independent Spirit Award nomination for Best Breakthrough Performance for her role as Carmen on Overcompensating. Her comedy brings a unique perspective on the strange banalities of entering the adult world as well as growing up with a strong multi-cultural Mexican-Syrian identity. She is also, unfortunately, Gen-Z.

Title: Address to a Haggis
Description: Fair fa’ your honest, sonsie face... Where better to hear Robert Burns' famous poem Address to a Haggis than at The Haggis Box Café in the Scottish Storytelling Centre! Drop in to hear a different surprise performer each day deliver a rousing rendition of Burns' ode to the Great Chieftain o’ the Puddin-race. Traditional, vegan and vegetarian haggis, neeps and tatties will be available to purchase all day with gluten-free options available. Haggis for all!
Artist: The Haggis Box / Scottish Storytelling Centre
Venue description: 2026 marks twenty years since the opening of the Scottish Storytelling Centre (SSC), the world's first purpose-built centre for oral storytelling and a space for creatives to explore culture and traditions from the ancient to the contemporary. You're invited to become part of the story all year round, whether enjoying a show, browsing the bookshop or refreshing yourself at the Haggis Box Café.

Title: Exhibition: Craigmillar Tapestry
Description: The Craigmillar Tapestry Project is a community initiative to create a series of tapestry panels representing the rich history of Craigmillar. Designed and stitched by local people with artwork and guidance from artist Andrew Crummy, there are now twenty panels stitched by over five hundred contributors. The panels are stitched to an incredibly high standard, reflecting the great talent in Craigmillar. People included elements of their own experience and cultures to the tapestries – such as traditional Syrian stitching, names of local activists and important landmarks.

Title: TSURU: My Crane Wife
Description: Where sound becomes movement in this reimagining of a classical Japanese folktale. Directed by Erica Yamada, a Toga Directors' Competition award recipient, the work features acclaimed performers who have been invited to stages across Asia. Praised in Japanese previews for its inventive movement, creativity and sound, the piece blends rhythm, myth and intimate storytelling into a visceral, cross-cultural experience that shifts from quiet physical poetry to contemporary dance and a powerful ensemble finale. Supported by the Great Britain Sasakawa Foundation.

Title: If We Really Were Witches
Description: What might’ve happened if real witches dropped in on the witch hunts? Comedy, we’re sure. Summoned by the ghost of a witch hunt victim, real witches Mildred, Agnes and Suds arrive to rescue innocent Obediently Snead and serve up justice of their own. When challenged by The Pricks of Puritanical Piety Guild and Social Club, the witches turn the tide on those who harm others out of ignorance and fear. This riotous four-person comedy makes its way to Edinburgh after premiering in New York City and selling out performances at the Scranton Fringe Festival.

Description: What is masculinity from a gay perspective? A one-man comedy about a mixed race gay guy, masculinity and breakups. Jordan, and his much smarter ‘professor’ alter ego, has just broken up with his first boyfriend, and has dreams of entering his healing era. Title: Alice Hawkins – Working Class Suffragette
Description: Great-grandson Peter Barratt with sister suffragette Ruth Pownall give a stirring and passionate account of working-class suffragette, Alice Hawkins, and her hard-fought campaign for the right to vote. Mother of six, lifelong socialist and shoe machinist by trade, Alice was arrested, imprisoned and almost forgotten, until now. As the UK approaches the centenary of working-class women gaining the vote, hear the suffragette history you were never taught and see her very own ‘Votes for Women’ sash, hunger strike medal, prison notes and more. Urgent, political and deeply human.**** (The Student Newspaper).
Artist: Great-Grandson Peter Barratt with Sister Suffragette Ruth Pownall

Title: Roses To The Living
Description: Pasuz Productions presents their new darkly comedic show about reputations and how you lose them, how one version of events becomes "the truth", and what your options are when your terribly worthy one-woman show is repeatedly interrupted by rowdy hecklers. This playful meta-theatrical piece juggles the stories of a well-meaning student, a director with a dark secret, a serially misunderstood monarch and a long dead literary giant. Who gets to tell their truth before the final curtain falls? (Do we have budget for a curtain? Join us to find out!).

Venue Accessibility



Physical Access to the Cameo



Both the bar and main entrance are wheelchair accessible. However, level access to the bar is only available from the street through the Lochrin Place entrance – moving between the two areas requires a wheelchair user to enter via the street.



Physical Access in the Screening Rooms



Screens 1 and 2 are accessible to customers with limited mobility, including wheelchair users. There are four wheelchair spaces in Screen 1 and two in Screen 2.



Dedicated wheelchair spaces are available in the following locations:



Screen 1: Row M, Seats 1-2 & 20-21



Screen 2: Row A, Seats 5-6 & 10-11



Aisles in our screens are located on each side of every row:



Screen 1: aisles are located next to seats A1 – M21 or seats A20, C20, E20, G20, J20, L20.



Screen 2: aisles are located next to seats A1-C1, A15, B16, and C18.



Sofa seats are double seats with no armrest in between. These are sold as two seats and are located:



Screen 1: No sofa seats



Screen 2: B1+2, B3+4, B13+14, B15+16, C1+2, C3+4, C15+16, C17+18



All seats have immovable armrests, and chairs are fixed together.



The distance of the aisles between seats – from the front of one row of seats to the back of another – is approximately 50cm. The seat base and back are approx 48cm wide; 69cm wide including armrests.



The sofa seats base and back are approximately 110cm wide; 133cm wide including armrests. These are sold as two separate seats.



Audio



All three screens are fitted with the Williams Sound hearing assistance headset system; please notify a member of staff if you wish to use a headset or induction loop compatible with a hearing aid.



Toilets



There is a fully accessible separate toilet for wheelchair users opposite the doors to Screen 1. There is an emergency call-point (the red hanging cord) inside should you need to call for assistance.



Assistance dogs



Assistance dogs are welcome at The Cameo Picturehouse. If you wish to take a dog into a performance, please let us know once you have booked your tickets, so we can ensure an aisle seat is reserved for you.



The Meadows is very close by for the exercise of assistance dogs. 



The bar is dog friendly and staff can provide water bowls and treats if the dogs are allowed.







Further Information

By Email: Use the email form on Picturehouse’s website here.

Description:
British sculptor Anne Hardy transforms Talbot Rice Gallery’s Georgian Gallery into a single immersive space, with sculptures made from cast elements, found materials and earth drawings. In this large-scale installation, Hardy constructs landscapes that are both human and post-human by animating the gallery with light, sound, data, and scenography. By grafting seemingly incompatible contexts into another, she considers how our bodies respond to space and sensory stimuli, creating an atmosphere that is responsive and alive with energy.

Description: Continuing the oral storytelling traditions of her lineage blended with theatre, Jenna Baer traces threads connecting generations. As the last Spider Witch, she weaves stories of five generations of her family: Appalachian healers, midwives, regular women and rebels who pass along their survival and power through folklore and folk medicine. Like a spider's web, inheritance doesn't move in straight lines. Knowledge skips generations, spirals, back, tangles and repairs itself. What do we inherit from those who came before us? What must we untangle to set ourselves free?

A powerful, visually striking exploration of independence, connection and fragile balance. Four bodies. One path. No way out alone.

Description: Soft Spot is a circus duet for a juggler, a handstand artist, wooden planks and 300 wine glasses. Everyone has held a wine glass. Everyone has broken one.
